newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-INSIDE CANBERRA - No poll until 1999.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-INSIDE CANBERRA - No poll until 1999.

text.p: (From the "Inside Canberra" newsletter)
CANBERRA, Dec 4 - John Howard does not need to hold an election until June 1999. Why then should he call a double dissolution in the first half of 1997?
A double dissolution in the first half of next year would mean after decades of struggle to get to the top he would be voluntarily giving up more than two years of his first term as Prime Minister.
Further, although he would win such an election, his massive majority would inevitably be heavily slashed, putting Labor in range of a win at the following election.
Despite its size, Howard's majority would disappear altogether with a uniform swing across the country of only 3.7 percent.

There is no pressing reason for the Government to go to a double dissolution, despite Peter Costello's theatrics over Senate resistance to a measure to deny new migrants certain welfare benefits for two years.
The Telstra sale legislation is a much bigger issue than this and we doubt whether Howard would think it worth a double dissolution.
He will undoubtedly send the bill on early migrant arrivals back to the Senate to give himself a double dissolution trigger which he can put into the bottom draw.

The PM will then be able to hold a double dissolution election in lieu of a normal election in late 1998 enabling him to get any measures through the Senate which failed to pass in the current Parliament's life, such as Telstra.

There are clear signs of a major shift within the Howard government away from the policies of economic rationalism, so unquestionably embraced by the Hawke and Keating governments, towards a far more pragmatic approach with the major focus on jobs, rather than inflation.
Of great importance was the announcement by John Howard at the Manila APEC summit that Australia's continued tariff reduction was conditional on reciprocal tariff cuts from its APEC trading partners.

Realising the economic rationalist lobby back home (with the Financial Review in the lead) would be after him, Howard told a Manila press conference how absurd it was for people to be "hyperventilating" about driving tariffs lower, with Australia so far in front of the field.
Demanding reciprocity was undoubtedly the most important policy decision taken by Howard since he became Prime Minister.

It reverses the (unstated) policy of the Keating government that Australian tariffs should be driven ever lower, irrespective of reciprocity by APEC countries because lower tariffs were in themselves good for the economy.

Thus Howard has embraced the view of Australian industry which was highly antagonistic to the government continuing to expose Australian producers to import competition whilst Australian exporters were blocked from access to Asian markets by non-tariff barriers.
The change of government policy will come as a great shock to the miners, and particularly the National Farmers Federation.

Only last week in the wake of the Clinton visit, NFF President, Donald McGauchie, stated: - "NFF is concerned about statements in our IAP (Individual Action Plan), that Australian tariff reductions may be dependent on the liberalisation commitments of other countries."
Tim Fischer is going to have some explaining to do to his electorate.
The change of course by the Howard government will come as no surprise to our readers and we have been giving pointers to it.

For example (Inside Canberra, April 12, 1995) we reported Howard, as Opposition Leader, telling the annual dinner of the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries last year: - "The proposition that Australia might find herself to be some kind of theoretical martyr to the goal of APEC without having obtained in return responses from countries of that region, is not something that commends itself to me."

And (Inside Canberra, September 13) we reported Howard at the meeting of APEC Energy Ministers in Sydney saying how difficult it was for politicians to carry out the dictum of trade liberalisation urged by economists.

And about the same time in a most interesting development, Treasurer, Peter Costello, in Washington, on this topic said: "...We therefore regard ourselves as having the right to ask for some mutuality and that's what we're doing".
-- Inside Canberra 61-6 273-1600
